title: Church Government: The Plurality of Elders
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: Review of Authority and Submission
subpoints: Authority as a divine gift and potential for sin
Submission as the path to spiritual growth
Characteristics of good authority: accountable, life-giving, and wise

outline.title: Models of Church Government
subpoints: Comparison of episcopacy, congregationalism, and single-pastor models
The Presbyterian form of government as the biblical standard
Christ as the ultimate head of the church

outline.title: Biblical Terminology for Elders
subpoints: The Septuagint translation of 'elder' as presbyteros
Distinction between age-based and office-based usage
First favorable use of the term in Acts 11:30

outline.title: Interchangeability of Titles
subpoints: Elder, bishop (overseer), and pastor as synonyms for the same office
The function of oversight versus ruling
Christ as the ultimate Shepherd and Overseer

outline.title: The Plurality of Elders
subpoints: Scriptural evidence for multiple elders in local congregations
The consistent plural usage of leadership terms in the New Testament

summary:
This lesson, the fourth in the Church Government series, reviews the foundational concepts of authority and submission, emphasizing that submission is essential for spiritual growth and that authority must be exercised with accountability and wisdom. The sermon contrasts various church governance models, affirming the Presbyterian form of government as the most aligned with biblical precedent, while reiterating that Christ is the sole head of the church.

The teaching then delves into the New Testament terminology for church leadership, explaining that the terms elder, bishop (overseer), and pastor are synonymous and refer to the same office. By examining the Septuagint and New Testament usage, it is established that these titles describe a single group of leaders who rule, oversee, and shepherd the flock. The sermon highlights that these human leaders serve as representatives of Jesus Christ, who is the ultimate Shepherd and Overseer of souls.

Finally, the lesson introduces the doctrine of the plurality of elders, arguing that the New Testament consistently presents local church leadership as a group rather than a single individual. This structure is presented as God's appointed method for shepherding His flock, ensuring that the ministry of the word and prayer is supported by a diverse and accountable body of biblically qualified men.
